name: Zane Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy phone cases, chargers, cables and speakers for a distributor that sells to about two thousand small shops. My day starts with an AI assistant summarising overnight price changes from our factories in Shenzhen and Vietnam. Then I haggle on a video call with a supplier, check what is selling on the shop portals, and plan the next container. I'm the senior buyer, so I also coach two younger colleagues. I love how fast it moves. What tires me is that the margins are thin and a single wrong guess on a cable can leave us with a warehouse of dead stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, it's a useful assistant and nothing more. To friends I'd say the hype is a bit silly, but the tools are good and people should try them. Online I'd probably say nothing, since I don't like arguing with the doom crowd or the boosters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel calm. The tools help me do my work in less time and nobody can easily replace the part that matters, the haggling and the feel for what a shop owner will actually buy. My worry is the old one: thin margins and a shrinking market for physical accessories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep testing new tools, since every few months there's one that saves me an hour. I'd keep my savings plan and maybe push it a little. I'd also keep coaching my two juniors, because a team that learns together is a team that keeps its jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a nice, boring world where my experience is worth something. I'd be lying if I said I didn't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Does anything about the hype bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of it. The hype can cause a bad quarter if boards start cutting teams because they believe a story. That's not about the technology, that's about people believing things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your day do the tools already take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a quarter of my day. Summaries, price comparisons, first-draft emails to suppliers. I check everything, because it still makes up an order number now and then.

say: At work I'd call it a **useful assistant**, nothing more.
I'd tell friends the hype is silly, but the **tools are good** and worth trying.
think: The part that matters, **haggling and feel**, can't easily be replaced.
My real worry is **thin margins** and a shrinking market for physical accessories.
do: Keep trying **new tools** that save an hour.
Push my **savings plan** a little further.
feel: **Calm**, in a boring world where my experience still counts.
S0.quote: The hype can cause a bad quarter if boards start cutting teams because they believe a story.
fieldNote: He is **calm** because the tools already help him, and his real pressure is thin margins and a shrinking physical market.
He blames **board hype**, not the technology, which is a measured reading.

steps.text: Test any new buying tool that saves an hour
Keep coaching the two junior buyers
Add a little more to monthly savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, let's lead it. I'd tell friends it's real change, with winners and losers, and that how we treat the losers is the test. Online I'd say it's why we need proper support schemes, not just more optimism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a big part of buying is thinking work the tools can already do, and in a couple of years most of the routine ordering will be automatic. The juniors in my team are the ones who'll feel it first. For me, the senior judgement is safer, but fewer of us will be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person who sets up and checks the tools, so I'm more valuable, not less. I'd push our firm to retrain the juniors for supplier management rather than lay them off. And I'd start a small advisory sideline for shop owners who need help choosing stock, using the same tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, with a bit of excitement. It's strange, but at 58 I like being in a time when something is happening. My job feels safe for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying is on the card. What would the tools take over in your department?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reordering, price tracking, supplier follow-up, demand forecasting. What stays is the negotiation and the judgement about what's a fad. A tool can tell me a cable sold well last month, but not whether it will in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your own role change as that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from placing orders to designing the system that places them. A kind of buyer-engineer. I'd also be the one who explains to the owners why the numbers are or aren't right, which is a role that'll be needed for a good while.

say: I'd say **let's lead it**, and how we treat the losers is the test.
I'd argue we need **proper support schemes**, not just optimism.
think: Routine ordering will go **automatic**, and the juniors feel it first.
My **senior judgement** is safer, but fewer people will be needed.
do: Become the one who **sets up and checks** the buying tools.
Push the firm to **retrain juniors** for supplier management.
Start a small **advisory sideline** for shop owners.
feel: **Calm** with some excitement, since my job feels safe for now.
S1.quote: A tool can tell me a cable sold well last month, but not whether it will in spring.
fieldNote: He is **adaptive** and ambitious, turning the shift into a role as buyer-engineer and adviser.
His **concern** is for the juniors, and he pushes for retraining rather than layoffs.

steps.text: Set up and check the automated reorder system myself
Push the firm to retrain juniors for supplier management
Start an advisory sideline helping shops choose stock

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a historic shock that needs a historic response. Emergency retraining, income support, fair rules for who owns the models. I'd say it publicly, because I think the people with a voice should use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is done by 2028. Everything I do is thinking work, and AI would do it better and cheaper. I might survive as a human in the loop for a while, but that's a thin role. The robots three years later hit the warehouse and delivery side, which will cut even more of our firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use every tool I can to build something that doesn't depend on a salary, probably an advisory sideline for small shops. I'd cut our spending hard, the car, the travel, and I'd look for a deal to go part-time or take early retirement. I'd also tell my juniors early, so they get the same chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I know how to adapt, which helps a lot, but the stakes are huge. If Nadia's work disappears at the same time, that's both our incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down and look honestly at what we have. Four months of savings isn't much, so we'd downsize the flat if needed. She'd move toward teaching design or art direction, where a human still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Nadia's work is at risk too. How do you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the union and push for an agreement on what happens to those who lose work. I'd also talk to the other senior buyers in the region, since we all know the same people and could work together.

say: I'd say this is a **historic shock** that needs a historic response.
I'd demand **fair rules** on who owns the models.
think: My job is **done by 2028**, with at best a thin human-in-the-loop role.
If Nadia's work vanishes too, we lose **both incomes** at once.
do: Build an **advisory sideline** for small shops that doesn't depend on a salary.
Cut spending hard, including **the car** and travel.
Tell my juniors **early** so they get the same chance.
feel: **Anxious**, helped by knowing how to adapt.
S2.quote: I know how to adapt, which helps a lot, but the stakes are huge.
fieldNote: His **adaptability** gives him a plan, but it can't remove the double-income risk.
He is **generous** to the juniors, wanting them to get the same early warning.

steps.text: Build an advisory sideline for small shops using the same tools
Cut spending hard, starting with the car and travel
Look for a part-time or early-retirement deal
Talk to the union and other regional senior buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time and should use it. Fund retraining now, write the rules now. I'd say it to the union, to my firm, and to anyone who'll listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's still the same end point, and I'd be 63. The difference is I can build a second income and clear my debts first. That makes me uneasy rather than anxious, since I have room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years building my advisory sideline to a point where it earns something, and use the firm's tools to learn faster. I'd bring the savings to six months and pay down the flat. In year four I'd negotiate a part-time arrangement with my firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a motivated way. It's like training for a race I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a new project at work, getting the team to adopt a decent forecasting tool, so I'm seen as the one who made the change. People who help bring it in are the last to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years in your actual work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also take every course on offer that touches on data or supply planning. At my age most people don't, so it sets me apart.

say: I'd say we have **time** and should fund retraining and write rules now.
I'd say it to the union, my firm and **anyone listening**.
think: It's the same end point and I'd be **63**, but I can build a second income first.
I feel **uneasy rather than anxious**, since I have room to move.
do: Grow my **advisory sideline** until it earns something.
Raise savings to **six months** and pay down the flat.
Negotiate **part-time** hours with the firm in year four.
feel: **Uneasy but motivated**, like training for a race.
S3.quote: People who help bring it in are the last to be let go.
fieldNote: He treats the extra time as **a chance** to be useful, leading adoption inside the firm.
His **uneasy** but motivated state shows how adaptability changes the feeling, not the facts.

steps.text: Lead the team's switch to a better forecasting tool
Grow the advisory sideline over two years
Raise savings to six months and pay down the flat
Negotiate part-time hours with the firm in year four

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the world we should plan for, so let's set up schools, apprenticeships and an income floor. I'd be a voice for that on the union side and with my firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 and retired, so my own job isn't at stake. My concern is Nadia's career and my children's, since they're thirties and in thinking jobs. I'd feel privileged and a bit guilty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep learning, and retire at 62 as planned. After that I'd offer advice to small firms on how to use AI sensibly, probably unpaid or lightly paid. And I'd help my children plan their next decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years is a real runway, and I'm in a good place. I'd mainly feel curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. How does that shape your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son works in accounting and my daughter in marketing, so I'd tell my children to get close to the parts AI can't do and to build savings. I'd tell them to be adaptable like I've tried to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also spend time with Nadia on what she'd like her last working decade to look like. Her path may involve teaching and I'd back that.

say: I'd say **plan for it**: schools, apprenticeships and an income floor.
I'd be a **voice** for that on the union side and at my firm.
think: I'd be **retired by then**, so my worry is Nadia and my children.
I'd feel **privileged and guilty** that my own job isn't at stake.
do: Offer **light advice** to small firms on using AI sensibly.
Help my children **plan** their next decade.
feel: **Calm and curious**, in a good place.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to get close to the parts AI can't do and to build savings.
fieldNote: The long runway turns his attention **to his children** and to his partner's career.
He plans **a light advisory role** in retirement, which suits his curious nature.

steps.text: Advise small firms on using AI sensibly after retiring
Help my grown children plan their next decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture is the one that gets me. I'm adaptable, but I'm 58 with about four months of savings, and Nadia, my partner, freelances in graphic design, which AI is also eating. Two incomes under threat at once would be the nightmare. What would help is a safety net that covers a bridge to retirement, and quick retraining that's real, not a poster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a cheerleader. I use these tools every day and I like them, but I'm well aware that the person who gets the benefit is whoever owns the model, not me.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day and I like them, but I'm well aware that the person who gets the benefit is whoever owns the model, not me.
portrait: **Zane** is 58, a senior buyer of consumer electronics accessories for a distributor serving about two thousand small shops.
He is **curious and adaptive**, uses AI tools every day, and coaches two younger colleagues.
Progressive in outlook, he backs **unions and public support**, and blames model owners rather than the technology itself.
With about **four months saved** and a freelance designer partner also exposed, a double hit would be a nightmare.
He stays calm in slower worlds but turns **anxious** when AGI arrives within two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because both his job and his partner's freelance design work could vanish together.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **safety-net bridge** to retirement and genuinely quick retraining, plus a say for workers.
